19814-three-years-in-france-with-the-gun:
Three Years in France with the Guns gives episodes in the life of a British artillery officer. One scene finds a subaltern waking from deep slumber in a train carriage. He peers out and groans at the beastly hole of Bouvette. His surprise at the laughter around him follows. The book's voice is dry, tired, and amused. It is the Western Front remembered by a gunner.

Artillery war was noise, mud, and long waiting between shoots. Officers' memoirs from the batteries are rarer than infantry ones. Episodes, rather than a grand narrative, suit that disjointed war. Humor carries scenes that horror would flatten. Readers get the guns' war at human scale. Such memoirs grounded Britain's memory of France.
19927-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for August 1862 is volume 2, number 2 of a wartime magazine. It declares itself devoted to literature and national policy. One story scene stands by a little run, four hundred yards from a farmhouse. A turpentine distillery occupies the bank there. Rosin and turpentine works scatter around it. Fiction, poetry, and war argument shared such numbers.

New York published the Continental through the Civil War's middle years. It mixed Southern scenes with Union politics deliberately. Turpentine country meant the pine barrens of the Carolinas. Stories grounded national policy in local color. A single issue shows the magazine's whole method. It remains useful to students of wartime print.
20565-the-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for August 1864, volume 6, number 2, mixes literature with the politics of a nation at war. The magazine spoke for the Union cause. Its essays scold the loose language of wartime debate as much as they praise the cause.

One writer complains that words like fool and tyrant are thrown at men the people have delighted to honor. Such language disgusts older and more thoughtful readers. It has become, he says, a recognized fact of the time. The issue shows how the Civil War filled even literary monthlies with argument about the nation's words and deeds.
22062-the-mathematicall-praeface-to-elem:
John Dee, Elizabeth I's famous astrologer-philosopher, wrote the Mathematicall Praeface for the first English Euclid in 1570. Henry Billingsley had translated the Elements of Geometrie; Dee's preface introduces it. He calls the preface very fruitful, specifying the chief mathematical sciences, what they are, and what they are good for. He also promises to disclose certain new mathematical and mechanical secrets, much missed until these days.

Dee maps arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, optics, music, and dozens of lesser arts in one great tree. He defends mathematics against charges of conjuring. The Praeface is a landmark of English science writing, and it made Dee's name across Europe. Readers still meet it as the gateway to Tudor mathematics.
22150-the-theories-of-darwin-and-their-r:
Eduard von Hartmann, the German philosopher, examined Darwin's theories and their bearing on philosophy, religion, and morals. His book, translated for English readers, addresses a troubled audience. Hartmann writes for people who feel they must set themselves right on these questions. They touch mankind's highest interests, yet few lay readers have time to master the sciences involved.

Hartmann argues that evolution and purpose need not be enemies. He defends a philosophy in which nature's process has meaning beyond blind chance. Religious and ethical views, he notes, remained sharply opposed after Darwin. The book is a period piece from the first great age of Darwin debates, when every thinker had to reckon with the new biology.
22690-rembrandt-and-his-works-comprising:
John Burnet wrote Rembrandt and His Works, a short account of the Dutch master's life and art, illustrated with examples from his etchings. The catalog record gives no year. Burnet, himself a painter and engraver, wrote for readers who admired Rembrandt but lacked access to the prints and paintings scattered across Europe.

In the preface, Burnet notes the limits set on the book's size and plates, while doing his publisher justice for sparing no expense to credit the great artist. Preparing the work showed him how wide the interest ran in making Rembrandt better appreciated. The text mixes biography with close looks at single etchings. It stands as an early English attempt to bring Rembrandt to a broad public, and it still reads with a practitioner's respect.
amenities-of-literature-consisting-of-sk:
Amenities of Literature, by Isaac Disraeli, collects sketches and characters of English literature. Disraeli, who wrote as Isaac D'Israeli and was the father of the prime minister, published the book in 1841 at the age of seventy-five; this edition dates from 1871. He meant it as a companion to his earlier Curiosities of Literature and Miscellanies of Literature.

The book was planned as part of a much larger work, a history of vernacular literature, that he never completed. What stands instead is a set of literary portraits and essays, written for pleasure by a lifelong man of letters. Readers get the elder Disraeli's hobby in bound form: anecdotal, curious criticism that preserves how the nineteenth century enjoyed its own literary past.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALangerWillia:
William L. Langer was Harvard's great diplomatic historian and, in wartime, the chief of research and analysis for the OSS, the CIA's forerunner. This Washington Post obituary by Richard Pearson marks his death and sums up the double career.

Langer wrote standard histories of European diplomacy and then ran the analysts who briefed a president, later chairing the CIA's Board of National Estimates. Pearson's obituary column in the Post kept a running record of Washington's passing generations. The obituary is kept as the paper's farewell to the historian and intelligence chief.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DavisThomasEli_: A handwritten note dated July 7, 1977 was sent to J. Gary Shaw of Cleburne, Texas. The note concerns Thomas Eli Davis and the assassination of President Kennedy. Its signature is illegible and the text survives only in fragments, so the writer cannot be identified and the full point of the message cannot be recovered from what remains.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIOfficeofProf: A study titled The Security Investigation examines the FBI's surveillance and harassment of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The Bureau's campaign against King is the whole subject: watching, listening, and pressure applied to the civil rights leader. The surviving record gives the study's title and subject but names no author or date, so it stands as a titled account of that campaign.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FulbrightJWilli:
A magazine profile titled The Roots of the Arkansas Questioner studies Senator J. William Fulbright of Arkansas. The profile centers on his role in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's Vietnam hearings. Fulbright, once a supporter of the war's architects, had become their most respectable questioner on Capitol Hill.

The hearings gave doubt about Vietnam a Senate stage and a courteous southern voice. A profile reaching for the roots of that stance asks where the questioner came from. The magazine and author are not identified in the record, but the piece preserves how Fulbright was presented to readers then.
govdocs-archive_org-tibetan-religion-tit:
Giuseppe Tucci, the great Italian Tibetologist, traced how Buddhism first spread through Tibet in his book Tibetan Religion. He follows the meeting between Indian Buddhism, arriving from the south, and Bon, the native religion already rooted in the high mountains.

Neither faith simply won. Tucci shows them mixing over centuries, borrowing gods, rites, and ideas until a distinct Tibetan Buddhism emerged from both. His learning rests on Tibetan texts, temple art, and years of travel in the region itself. The book is a landmark of Asian studies, and the full text gives readers his account whole, from the first diffusion of Buddhism onward.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cybervault_Cyber_: Israel built one of the world's most admired cybersecurity establishments, pairing military units that train teenage hackers with a startup sector that sells their skills worldwide. A National Security Archive cyber brief, published on May 22, 2018, surveys that establishment and its record. The brief sits in the Archive's Cyber Vault, which collects the public and declassified record of how states organize for conflict in cyberspace. For readers comparing national models, Israel is the standard case of a small country turning compulsory service and technical education into strategic weight online.
nasa-tm-19650010163-the-role-of-research:
John L Sloop, NASA's assistant associate administrator for advanced research and technology, gave this lecture on October 22, 1964. He spoke to Santa Clara County science teachers at Ames Research Center. His subject was the part research plays in crewed space flight.

Sloop frames the Moon landing plan as one step in a longer process. He says reaching that goal would boost science and technology, and national prestige and security. He also links space work to daily life. The lecture shows how NASA explained its research program to teachers in 1964. For teachers, that link between classroom science and national goals was the practical point of the talk.
nasa-tm-19680010567-a-mission-tracking-c:
Goddard Space Flight Center's Tracking and Data Systems Directorate produced this study in September 1967. It is the directorate's contribution to Phase A of the Galactic Jupiter Probe study at Goddard. Phase A was the early planning phase for the proposed deep space mission. The report presents a mission analysis together with the tracking, communication, and flight operation studies that support it.

A study cadre from the directorate carried out the work under cadre leader Richard Lehnert. Chapters were chaired separately for mission analysis, ground network support, communication and data handling, and flight operations. The catalog record names the supporting topics. They include ground network help, trajectory and guidance work, and flight operations. All support a spacecraft billions of kilometers away. Together the chapters ask what it would take, from the ground, to fly a probe to Jupiter.
nasa-tm-19700015586-relative-motion-of-t:
E. R. Lancaster of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in April 1970. It treats the relative motion of two particles, each moving in its own elliptic orbit under gravity. Work of this kind helps predict how two orbiting bodies drift toward or away from each other over time.

Lancaster notes that papers over the past decade offered only approximate solutions to this problem. Those solutions assumed the gap and speed difference between the particles stay small beside their own positions and speeds. His paper works through the problem with a full set of defined symbols and orbit terms. A worked numerical example near the end shows the method in use.
nasa-tm-19700030131-glossary-of-terms-pe:
The Kennedy Space Center issued this glossary in June 1970. It defines the terms used in reliability and quality assurance work at the center. Staff across many offices needed one shared set of meanings for their checks and reviews.

Entries run from basic ideas, such as acceptable quality level, onward through the field. The acceptable quality level is given as a rate of defects that a batch may show. The book was kept current by the center's Quality Assurance Directorate. Changes and supplements were issued as the need arose. A shared vocabulary keeps inspection fair and reports clear.
nasa-tm-19720004489-redundancy-managemen:
Richard A Campbell of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 9, 1971, as NASA TM X-64625. He worked in the Astrionics Laboratory. The subject is backup management for electrohydraulic servoactuators. These powered units move control surfaces and engine parts. If one fails in flight, a spare must take over cleanly. Campbell's system watches for that moment using mathematics, not extra sensors.

A mathematical model of a healthy actuator runs beside the real ones. A compensation network adjusts the model for outside disturbances. When a real unit drifts from the model, the system can flag the fault. It can then switch control to a sound spare. The report presents the full model reference design.
podcast-dannyjones-CwcIqRaSbLI:
Anjan Katta works on technology designed to cut the health costs of screens. He brings Danny Jones a warning attributed to Steve Jobs. In that warning, blue light from devices is making people sick. Katta argues Jobs limited his own children's screen time because he understood what the light does to eyes, sleep, and brains.

The episode covers the biology as Katta presents it: circadian rhythms broken by evening light, eye strain, and the deeper effects he links to modern disease. Jones tests the claims against his own habits, as listeners will. Some of the science here, light and sleep, is well established; the larger claims are Katta's. The conversation works as a practical brief for changing how a household uses screens, whatever a listener decides about its strongest assertions.
podcast-dannyjones-WMnIyiFnlLI:
Randall Carlson tells Danny Jones why humans need to leave Earth soon, in an entry from the Danny Jones podcast. Carlson, the catastrophist who studies cosmic impacts, argues that our planet's calm is a lucky break that will end. Jones hosts him in a long, curious interview format.

Carlson lays out the record of past strikes and what one large impact would do to cities, farms, and climate. He argues that spreading to other worlds is not adventure but insurance. The talk gives his warning its starkest form, and it suits listeners who met him on Rogan's show and want the pure case.
podcast-dannyjones-WmD3uDMH7LI:
Dr. Rick Strassman, the best known researcher of the drug DMT, joins Danny Jones for a long talk. The episode title ties his secret research to biblical prophecy and the CIA. Strassman ran early legal studies in which volunteers took DMT under watch.

Strassman tells what his volunteers reported, including beings they said they met while on the drug. The talk moves from lab results to scripture and to claims about agency interest in his work. Listeners hear a rare mix of hard lab work and open wonder. The library keeps the episode as an archive record, without judging the claims.
podcast-tuckercarlson-LaH2QalhJLI:
Bret Weinstein is the evolutionary biologist who left academia in a famous campus fight. He sits with Tucker Carlson to debate the largest questions either man hosts. They include evolution itself, the existence of God, and Israel. They also include whether artificial intelligence will gain consciousness. The conversation is billed as a debate, and both men arrive with positions.

Weinstein argues from biology toward a cautious openness on faith; Carlson argues from conviction toward the gaps in materialism. Their exchange on Israel places an ally of the country beside one of its sharpest critics on the right. Nothing is settled, which is the format's honesty. The recording preserves two of independent media's biggest names testing each other's worldviews at length, a specimen of the long-form argument that replaced the television segment for their shared audience.
rico-and-wiseli:
Johanna Spyri's tales of Swiss children appear here in Louise Brooks's translation, in two stories bound together. The first, Rico and Stineli, runs to twenty-one chapters in the contents. The second, How Wiseli Was Provided For, follows it and gives the volume its joint title.

Rico's story moves from a quiet house and school days to the old schoolmaster's fiddle. A beautiful, distant lake without a name draws him, and a sad house gives the lake a name at last. Chapters on his mother, a precious legacy, and a long journey lead to the Lake of Sils and then to sunshine on the Lake of Garda. Two happy travellers cross the mountains home.
ten-years-exile-memoirs-of-that-interest: The Baroness de Stael-Holstein wrote Ten Years' Exile. She set the memoirs down in 1810, 1811, 1812, and 1813. Her son first printed them from her own manuscript. Treuttel and Wurtz of London issued the book in 1821. The text was rendered from the French. Chapter heads name the causes of Bonaparte's enmity. They name strife in the Tribunate and Fouche. They name the Marengo campaign and the Infernal Machine. The Peace of Luneville, Paris in 1801, and a trip to Coppet follow.
the-latin-irish-lives-of-ciaran-translat:
R. A. Stewart-Macalister edited early lives of Saint Ciaran for a Christian literature series, issued in London and New York in 1921. The contents promise a harmony of four lives, three Latin lives, an Irish life, notes, and a Latin text. His scholarly pages discuss manuscripts held in the Bodleian Library.

Two manuscripts, Rawlinson B 485 and B 505, carry the second Latin life, and one copies the other directly. Scholars disagree on their dates by more than a century. Readers interested in Celtic saints get both translated lives and the source problems behind them, set out in plain academic detail.
the-new-machiavelli: H. G. Wells's 1911 novel about Richard Remington, a brilliant politician whose career collapses over a love affair. Part political roman à clef, part Wellsian sermon on the need for a planned society, it scandalized readers with its frankness. Ambitious and uneven, it is Wells baring his own soul.
